I am 63 years old, and I have been farming these lands in Quzhou since I was a young man. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. My father and grandfather before me farmed this same soil, and I know what works here on the North China Plain.

This year, I will stick to what I know best: **winter wheat followed by summer maize**. That is the double-cropping system my family has always used. The wheat goes in after National Day in October, sleeps through the winter, and comes up green in spring for harvest around early June. The day after we cut the wheat, we plant maize. Every day counts in the summer season — if we are late, the frost will get us before the cobs are dry.

I have 6 mu of good flat land. I will plant all of it to wheat this winter, and then all of it to maize in the summer. I will buy improved wheat seed from the county supply store — I have used the same variety for years, and it does well here. For the maize, I use hybrid seed. The hybrids yield more, and nowadays the seed dealers bring them right to the village. I never save my own maize seed anymore; the hybrids do not breed true, and I learned that lesson long ago.

For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing for both crops, then top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring and again at jointing. The maize gets a big dose of nitrogen at the V6 stage, when it is growing fast. I do not bother much with potassium — the soil here has enough, I think — but I add a little because the shop says it helps. I till with the rotary tiller before each crop. No-tillage might save fuel, but I do not trust the weeds, and I like to see a clean seedbed.

Water is precious. We pump from the groundwater. The wheat needs three good irrigations: once before winter to help it establish, once at jointing in March or April, and once at heading. The maize needs two irrigations if the summer rains are kind — one at knee-high and one at tasseling. If the rains fail, maybe three.

I spray pesticides when I see aphids or the leaf rust coming. Usually two or three times on the wheat, and twice on the maize. I walk the fields every morning. That is how I know.
